1:
The chapter opens with a command, and the commentators dwell on the imperative. John Calvin says the imperative is more forcible than plain narrative, because the prophet addresses her as if from the judgment-seat, publishing what shall happen with the boldness his commission entitles him to—the authority by which a prophet is set over nations and kingdoms to root out and pull down. He explains why the oracle stands here: no hope of return could be entertained while the Babylonian monarchy flourished, so the prophet connects its overthrow with the deliverance that followed, the rank of that city having been like a deep grave in which the Jews were buried. Matthew Henry hears the words as a warning rather than a sentence, a message sent to Babylon like that of Jonah to Nineveh, fair warning given that she may by repentance prevent the ruin. He begins from the controversy itself, since there all the calamity begins: she has made God her enemy, and then who can befriend her? Were it a man who would be revenged on us we might hope to escape him, but this is not the strength of a man, easily resisted, nor the justice of a man, which may be bribed or mollified by a foolish pity, but the power and justice of God, which cannot be evaded.

The title virgin is glossed by nearly everyone, and not alike. John Gill takes it to mean the monarchy had never been subdued from its first setting up until it fell to Cyrus, citing a historian for the claim that this was the first time Babylon was taken, and to mark its beauty and glory. Calvin refuses the moral sense outright: she is called virgin not because she was modest or chaste, but because she had been brought up softly and had never been forced. John Wesley says only that she was tender and delicate, and that the empire is translated to the Persians. Charles Ellicott makes the epithets a comment on her habits, suggesting wanton as a better rendering than tender and finding in both the luxury identified with Babylon which was now to cease. Adam Clarke sets out the chapter’s design—a beautiful selection of circumstances in which her prosperous condition is contrasted with her adverse, a delicate female reduced to the abject condition of a slave—and observes that almost all its imagery is applied in the Revelation, in nearly the same words, to the antitype of the Chaldean capital. Gill reports the same identification from an earlier father, that some interpret the passage of Rome as mystical Babylon, and applies the threat to the papal church.

The tasks of the second verse are read as a picture of slavery, and the commentators supply the social detail. Clarke insists that grinding was not merely the work of slaves but the hardest of it, often inflicted as a punishment, and quotes Latin comic verse in which the mill, the scourge and the stocks stand together, a delinquent being called a man worthy of the mill; he notes that water-mills were not invented until shortly before the time of Augustus and windmills long after, and that in the east the work fell to female slaves. Ellicott calls it the most servile form of female labour, and says the picture is heightened by the slave having to wade unveiled and bare-legged, all sense of shame outraged, to the scene of her labours—symbolically, he adds, not literally. Gill and Wesley read the command as a prediction that the Chaldeans should themselves be taken captive and set to servile work. Calvin draws the reversal out: believers need not doubt they shall freely depart when the Babylonians who held them are themselves imprisoned; and the curled locks are named because of their indulgence in magnificence of dress, so that filth shall now cover those who once dazzled all eyes with gaudy finery.
3:
The exposure threatened is read as the removal of a covering that hid more than a body. John Calvin makes it the conclusion of the foregoing statement: so long as Babylon flourished she preserved her reputation, for wealth and power, like veils, conceal a great number of sores which become visible and are beheld with the greatest disgrace once the veils are removed. He quotes Demosthenes on the condition of Philip to the same effect—that no malady is perceived in any member while a person is in full vigour, but if he fall into debility the whole body is affected, and so with cities and governments. When wealth and troops are taken away, the disgraceful transactions that lay concealed are exposed: cruelty, fraud, extortion, perjury and unjust oppression, all honoured during prosperity, now fall into disgrace. John Gill keeps the literal picture of a sacked city, the conquered stripped by the soldiers, and adds the parallel of the mystical Babylon whom the kings of the earth make desolate and naked. John Wesley offers both readings of the uncovering, for want of raiment or by enemies in scorn.

The clause that follows is agreed to be difficult, and each resolves it differently. Charles Ellicott points out that the words supplied in italics show as much, and that omitting them yields either I shall not meet a man—none will oppose me—or I will not spare one. Adam Clarke proposes a change of pointing that would make the verb causative and give the sense that God will not suffer man to intercede with him. Calvin reports both without choosing: some supply a comparative particle, so that the meaning is do not think you have to deal with a man whose attack you may resist, since elsewhere the hand of man denotes some abatement, whereas here no remedy is left; others translate it as a refusal to allow any meeting at all. Wesley takes the simplest sense, that God will not deal with her with the moderation of men who have not put off humanity.

The short verse about the Redeemer is felt to interrupt the sentence, and the explanations differ in kind. Clarke describes it formally, as a chorus breaking in with a change of construction as well as of sentiment, moving to a shorter verse for one distich only, after which the former style is resumed. Ellicott allows that it comes in abruptly and considers whether it was a marginal addition that found its way into the text, but prefers to view it as Israel’s song of praise over the overthrow of Babylon, with a parallel in the fall of the mystical Babylon in the Revelation. Gill reads it as the words of the Lord’s people expressing faith in what has been foretold and in their own deliverance. Calvin gives it a purpose rather than a form: the prophet shows why the Lord inflicts this punishment, for the salvation of his people, and speaks abruptly, like a person awakened out of sleep, on seeing Babylon ruined that once trampled other nations under her feet.

The command to sit silent reverses her old voice. Calvin observes that while she reigned she cried with a loud voice and terrified the whole East by her commands; now she will not venture terrific words, nor even a gentle sound. He weighs whether the silence marks shame or subjection and adopts the former, since those whose condition has changed for the worse shut their mouth through shame. Gill draws the same contrast from her reputation: a place of noise and hurry, talked of all the world over, now buried in oblivion and sitting as a mourner. Ellicott sets the stir of the rejoicing city against the stillness of its desolation, and says the lady of kingdoms—almost, he suggests, the empress—was reduced to the loneliness of widowhood. Wesley reads the silence as grief and shame together.
6:
The first reason given is that Babylon exceeded her commission. John Gill puts it plainly: God was angry with his people for their idolatries, yet resented their ill usage. John Calvin makes the point do double duty. The first clause calls the Jews to repentance, since by their own crimes they drew down these calamities—had the scourge come from another hand, there would be no remedy in God’s. The second accuses the Babylonians of seizing the occasion for cruelty, as if one became the executioner of a child whom a father had put into his hands; they have no right to be proud as though they had subdued the Jews by their own power. Adam Clarke states the principle as a rule of providence: God uses conquerors and tyrants to execute his judgments, employing one wicked nation to scourge another, and the inflicter may be as culpable as the sufferer, adding to his guilt by indulging his cruelty; when he has fulfilled the work, he becomes himself the object of it. Charles Ellicott and John Wesley fix on the aggravation named in the verse, that she cast off reverence for age and laid her yoke heavily on the old, who besides the common calamity bore the miseries of age.

The second charge is the boast of permanence. Calvin censures the haughtiness of promising themselves perpetual dominion; the children of this world are intoxicated by prosperity, and it is madness when men, forgetting their frailty, look on themselves as not sharing the common lot, for so they forget that they are men. Believers too are persuaded they are safe under God’s hand, yet do not cease to consider that they are liable to many distresses, since nothing here is lasting. He notes that the verb means to conclude in one’s own mind, since proud men do not speak this way publicly but hold the conviction while pretending otherwise; a Jewish commentator paraphrases it, that she thought she would perpetually be mistress and go unpunished. Gill hears mystical Babylon say she sits a queen and shall see no sorrow. Ellicott says her confidence in her own perpetuity blinded her to the divine law that pride and cruelty bring their own Nemesis. Clarke leaves the sense alone and works on the text, proposing two emendations from manuscripts—one making the particle causal, the other making the latter end hers rather than its—and noting that one of his oldest manuscripts lacks both this verse and the one before.

The third charge is self-deification. Matthew Henry observes that the words she says in her heart are the very words God has often said of himself, denoting his self-existence and sole supremacy; it is presumption to say of any creature that there is none besides it, and arrogance to say it of oneself—and since Babylon made what gods she pleased for the people to worship, no wonder she made herself one among them. He notes that the boast is repeated, which intimates she said it often and that it was offensive to God. Ellicott says the boasts are purposely framed to recall the Lord’s own assertion of his eternity, so that she practically deified herself, and notes a like boast in the mouth of Nineveh, repeated almost verbally by Martial of Rome. Calvin resolves the claim into three: that she alone is, which none but God can truly say; that the world does not deserve comparison with her; and that she promises herself endless repose. Keil and Delitzsch mark the strophe opening here on the ground of the conduct censured, and note the answer implied—that the two things she says she will never know, bereavement and widowhood, will come upon her suddenly in one day and in fullest measure, in spite of all her sorceries. Wesley glosses the boast as independence and self-sufficiency, the security as never wanting a king or people to defend her.
9:
The two losses she said she would never know are promised together; the commentators agree on the suddenness and differ on the history. John Gill recalls that the destruction was very sudden, the city taken by surprise while the king and his nobles were at a feast; that night Belshazzar was slain and Darius the Mede took the kingdom, so that she lost king and royal family at once. He cites Xenophon for the report that when Cyrus took the city not only the king was slain but those about him, the inhabitants being ordered to keep within doors and all found without to be slain; another scholar, he notes, refers the prophecy rather to the later siege under Darius, when the besieged killed their own women to save provisions. Adam Clarke reads the widowhood as metaphorical, the governor being the husband and Belshazzar slain, and adds that Darius is said to have crucified three thousand of the principal inhabitants. John Calvin presses the word rendered in their perfection to mean completely, so that in all points she shall be childless, and finds an implied contrast between a moderate punishment, some alleviation of which may be expected, and a vengeance which has no end but ruin—the greater the confidence with which wicked men are elated, the more severely they are punished.

Two questions of rendering divide them. On the phrase in their perfection Charles Ellicott prefers in their completeness, saying she should taste the full bitterness of widowhood and bereavement, and John Wesley glosses it in the highest degree; Clarke prefers a different word, reporting that the Greek and Syriac translators read suddenly in their copies, which would balance the phrase in a moment in the preceding clause, and holding that their concurrent testimony may safely be opposed to the present text. On the particle before the multitude of sorceries, Clarke and Ellicott render it in spite of rather than because of. Calvin canvasses the same question and reports the state of opinion: some take it to express a cause, making the occult arts a fresh charge and a new reason for the destruction, while others make it concessive, so that the clause simply declares superstitious arts insufficient to save them. He inclines to a third course, giving the particle its proper sense, and takes the sorceries as naming the act rather than the practitioners.

The trust reposed in wickedness is examined for what it assumes. Calvin extends the word beyond magic to the fraud, oppression and violence by which the Babylonians raised themselves to such power: almost all large kingdoms are, as a distinguished robber once pronounced them, great robberies, since there is no other way of enlarging dominion than by extorting it from others and driving out the lawful owners. What the prophet calls malice is what tyrants adorn with more plausible names, laying aside all regard to justice and cunningly deceiving the people; but the Lord exposes them, so that covering wickedness with useless veils is seen to serve no purpose. On the boast that none sees, he observes that while men are kept to their duty by fear or shame, one who neither dreads God as a witness nor thinks men will know what he does breaks out into every licentiousness; even the worst are often tormented by conscience, but by shutting their eyes they plunge into stupidity as into a lurking-place. Gill lists the same objects of trust—wealth and power wickedly obtained, political schemes wickedly contrived, ambition, tyranny and cruelty, and especially astrology, divination and magic. Ellicott states the principle: Babylon, like other nations that followed in her steps, took for its law that might was right, practically denied the existence of a Ruler who saw and judged, and boasted of its wisdom—which the context shows to be astrology and magic. Wesley notes that the boast is repeated, to denote their intolerable self-confidence.
11:
The threefold evil announced here is the hardest sentence in the chapter to translate, and Adam Clarke makes the difficulty the point. He renders the first clause thou shalt not know how to deprecate it, following an ancient version, and translates the whole literally to display the gap: evil shall come and thou shalt not know how to deprecate it, mischief shall fall and thou shalt not be able to expiate it, destruction shall come suddenly and thou shalt not know. A word appears to be wanting at the end of that clause: not know what? how to escape it, to be delivered from it? He is persuaded a phrase has been lost, but since the ancient versions retain no trace of it he has not tried to fill the gap, only palliating a defect he cannot supply. Charles Ellicott gives two renderings proposed for the middle clause—of which thou shalt know no dawn, after the night of calamity, or which thou shalt not be able to charm away—and observes that the stress falls on the destruction being at once unforeseen and irretrievable. John Calvin ridicules the confidence of those who thought that by the position of the stars they foresaw all events, and applies the general threat of Scripture, that when they shall say peace and safety, sudden destruction shall overwhelm them, and at daybreak they shall not know what the evening will bring. John Gill and John Wesley note that the history agrees, Babylon being surprised in deep security.

The challenge that follows is heard as irony, and they differ only on its temper. Gill calls it an ironic expression deriding these arts and calling on their masters to do their utmost. Ellicott finds a subtle irony in the twice-repeated perchance—perchance thou wilt profit, perchance thou wilt strike terror. Keil and Delitzsch place the verse structurally, as the opening of the concluding strophe which, like the first, announces the city’s fate in a triumphantly sarcastic tone, whereas the intervening strophes name the sins that brought it on; others, they note, render the opening word persevere rather than come near. Calvin hears the way one speaks to desperate men on whom no warning takes effect—do as thou art wont, and the event will instruct thee—and finds in the word stand an allusion to the augurs, who remain unmoved in one place until some sign is seen, as the astrologers mark their divisions in the heavens to the minutest points. Wesley notes that the labour is dated from the beginning of her kingdom, the Chaldeans being in all ages famous for these arts.

The weariness of many counsels is turned against the counsellors. Gill identifies them as the astrologers, diviners and soothsayers who could never answer the questions put to them, instancing the consultation about the dream and the one about the writing on the wall, on the very night the city was taken. Calvin draws a general rule: the prophet says not counsels merely but a multitude of counsels, to show there is no reason for being puffed up whatever one’s ingenuity, since crafty counsels annoy their authors the more numerous they are. God scatters the contrivances of those who, trusting their own ability, collect every stratagem for oppressing others; such consultations fail because they do not ask counsel of God, and the more they toil the greater their annoyance. Ellicott explains the three titles as two aspects of one art, the dividers of the heavens who assign stellar influences to the signs of the Zodiac, and the star-gazers who make known things to come at the new moon; the Assyrian and Babylonian observers, he adds, compiled an almanack noting the days of the month as lucky or unlucky for war or home life. Clarke proposes an emendation here too, dividing one word into two on the Greek version’s authority to yield what is to happen to thee.
14:
The image chosen for the diviners is read as deliberately dismissive. John Calvin notes that the prophet does not compare them to wood, which is of some use for giving heat, but to stubble, in order to show that nothing is so light or useless; and he explains the vehemence by what such men do to religion. Impostors of this sort take away all fear of God out of the hearts of men by ascribing everything to the stars, so that nothing is left to his providence; from this arises contempt of God and of all his threatenings, since punishments are ascribed not to his judgment but to some fate they foolishly imagine. John Gill keeps the comparison at the same level: these astrologers and diviners shall be weak as stubble, no more able to stand before the fire of divine wrath, or before the judgments of God by the hands of the Medes and Persians, than stubble before a fire. Charles Ellicott presses the second half of the verse, correcting the rendering so that the clause describes the flame rather than the men: the destroying flame shall be altogether other than the fire on the hearth at which a man can sit and warm himself.

The last verse is the most contested in the chapter, because it turns on who is meant by those with whom she laboured. Calvin takes the word as a metaphor from merchants, skilled in innumerable arts of deceiving, so that the princes traffic in disgraceful transactions rather than consulting in a manner suitable to their rank; and though the term may be extended to all the allies who aided the Babylonians, he says the prophet has his eye chiefly on the diviners. He reports the alternatives fairly: it is a question whether these are traders in the ordinary sense, or national allies and negotiators, or whether the epithet is given in contempt to the astrologers of the foregoing context as dealing in imposture. One scholar he cites supposes them travelling dealers, pedlars and hawkers who moved from place to place lest their frauds be discovered, comparing them with the fortune-tellers of his own day while admitting that the astrologers of Babylonia held a very different position. Ellicott takes the plain commercial sense: the commerce of Babylon is prominent in all descriptions, a Greek historian and the prophet Ezekiel being cited for it; the time was coming when those who had thronged her markets would desert her and leave her to her desolation.

Gill and John Wesley divide over the same clause. Gill keeps them the diviners, those whom she had laboured in training up in these arts and consulting in cases of difficulty, who were of no service then and in the time of danger are as useless as stubble or a blaze of straw. Wesley proposes a rearrangement instead, taking the verse to contain two matters rather than one: thus vain and unprofitable shall thy sorcerers, with whom thou hast laboured, be unto thee—and then a fresh subject, that thy merchants, they with whom thou hast traded from thy youth, shall wander every one to his own quarter. He defends the transposition of words as nothing more than usual in Scripture, and identifies the merchants as those who came from several countries to trade with Babylon. Adam Clarke ends on a textual note, remarking that expositors give no very good account of the final phrase, and reporting that in a manuscript the word was at first written so as to mean to his servant or to his work, which he takes for the true reading. The sense, he allows, comes out much the same as the common interpretation: every one shall turn aside to his own business, and none shall deliver thee.
